1.pericope_label: The high priest asks: are these things so?

schools.summary: Allow some colour of justice, since the accused was permitted to defend himself, and set out what the question actually charged — the destruction of the temple and the changing of the customs.

Allow only a show of fairness, the president having prejudged the case; and turn from the question to the speaker, who is ready and mighty in the Scriptures, inferring from the abrupt ending that the speech is incomplete.

Grant a colour of equity and withdraw it, since the court asks not what warrant the teaching had but only whether the words were said; press the parallel with the tribunals of a later age; and answer the objection that the reply is long and irrelevant by showing that the charge of apostasy is met throughout.

Match the question to a formal arraignment; explain the historical method by the impossibility of answering the two charges yes or no, and by what such an audience would consent to hear; and defend the report of the speech as genuine on grounds of style and of who was present to preserve it.

debates: How far the question was a fair one: some colour of justice (Clarke), a show of fairness masking a prejudged case (Henry), or a colour of equity that collapses on inspection into a demand for a confession (Calvin).

Why the defence is historical rather than direct: because the charges admitted no simple answer (Robertson), because the history itself proves the belief denied him and secures a hearing (Barnes), or because the apparent irrelevance is only apparent (Calvin, answering the objection he raises against himself).
Whether the speech as we have it is complete — Henry and Barnes both infer from the interruption that it is not.
outliers: Calvin alone reads the high priest’s procedure as the pattern of a later inquisition and names the penalty it ends in.
Robertson alone argues for the authenticity of the speech against the view that it was composed by the historian, and names the witnesses who could have preserved it.
Barnes alone explains the choice of subject by what the audience was willing to listen to.

2.pericope_label: The God of glory appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia; get thee out of thy country; his removal after his father died

schools.summary: Judge the speech an interrupted fragment whose incompleteness argues for the genuineness of the report, probably derived from Paul; take the opening title as itself a refutation of the charge of blasphemy; and set out the chronological difficulty about Terah with its several solutions, one commentator conceding that the speaker held only to the broad outline and another that no explanation is certain.

Correct the rendering of the address, which names two classes and not three; and harmonise the chronology by supposing Abraham to have lived partly with his father and partly in Canaan until his father’s death.

Distinguish this call, spoken in Mesopotamia, from the later one; explain why the title of fathers is conceded to an unjust court and how far such deference reaches; read the deferred showing of the land as the trial of faith; and account for the stay at Charran by the father’s sickness.

debates: Whether the words quoted in the third verse are the call recorded in Genesis or an earlier and distinct one — Gill and Lightfoot argue for two calls from the absence of “thy father’s house”, Barnes assumes one.

How the sixty years between Abraham’s departure and Terah’s death are to be accounted for: a textual error (Barnes), Abraham named first for honour rather than age (Ellicott, Robertson), a harmonising of the two residences (Wesley), or an inexactness in the speaker’s own recollection (Ellicott’s preference) — with Robertson holding that no solution is certain.
How many classes the opening address names, and whether the received English misrepresents it (Clarke against the common rendering).
Whether the report of the speech is trustworthy — Ellicott argues from its very incompleteness that it is.
outliers: Ellicott alone prefaces the speech with a critical estimate of its transmission, and alone prefers an explanation of the chronology that concedes inexactness in the speaker.
Calvin alone asks on what terms an honourable title may be conceded to a hostile tribunal, and turns the answer against the courts of his own day.
Lightfoot alone attacks the Greek translators of the genealogy for adding a death to every name in it.
Wesley alone reduces the argument of the whole speech to the priority of promise over law and of law over temple.

5.pericope_label: No inheritance, not so much as a foot’s tread; the four hundred years foretold; the covenant of circumcision

schools.summary: Distinguish what was bought from what was given; weigh the competing reckonings of the sojourn and conclude that chronological precision is not to be looked for, no solution being certain; note that the closing words of the seventh verse are transferred from Horeb to Canaan and explain it by the freedom of recollection; read the argument as a threat to the persecutors’ tenure of the land; and state exactly what the speaker concedes and what he asserts about circumcision.

Explain the four hundred years as a round number dropping the odd tens, as writers not professedly chronological always do; distinguish the three acts of a judge and fix the sense here as punishment; and take the purchase of a burial field as itself a proof of the buyer’s strangerhood.

Draw from the empty-handed patriarch that a possession answering none of the uses of this life is none, and that the promise is the stay where the thing is wanting; join the judgement of the oppressor to the deliverance of the oppressed; and argue from the priority of the call and the promise that salvation does not begin in the outward sign.
Press the long interval as proof that delay does not falsify a promise, and exclaim that through all those years of promise there was neither sacrifice nor circumcision.

debates: How the four hundred years are to be reconciled with the four hundred and thirty: a round number with the tens dropped (Clarke), an unresolved perplexity (Barnes), a difference traceable to the Greek and Samaritan texts and not to be settled precisely (Ellicott), or a question no solution answers (Robertson).
Whether the closing words of the seventh verse belong to Horeb or to Canaan — Robertson and Ellicott agree the source refers to Horeb and differ on how deliberate the transfer is.

What the mention of circumcision concedes: Ellicott alone holds that the speaker does not deny having taught that the customs would be changed, and that his point is the priority of promise over sign rather than the abolition of the sign.
Whether the argument about the land is historical or minatory — Lightfoot alone reads it as a warning that possession is not unconditional.
outliers: Lightfoot alone turns the patriarchs’ landlessness into a direct threat against the hearers’ title to the country.
Chrysostom alone argues from the four hundred years to the delay of the kingdom rather than to a chronological problem.
Ellicott alone concedes that the speaker’s recollection is free rather than exact, and does so twice in these four verses.
Clarke alone disposes of the chronological difficulty by a convention of ordinary usage rather than by textual or historical argument.

9.pericope_label: The patriarchs sell Joseph; Jacob goes down into Egypt with seventy-five souls; the burial at Sychem

schools.summary: Trace the seventy-five to the Greek version and, in one case, concede that the speaker took it from that version without investigating; canvass the traditions about the patriarchs’ graves, preferring a Samaritan one; decline to choose between the competing authorities; and entertain the possibility that the received text is corrupt and that a different name should stand in it.

Name the persons the Greek version inserts; and explain the burial verse as a compression of two purchases and two graves into one sentence, a concise manner of speaking usual among the Hebrews where the story was well known.

Raise the possibility that the number was not written deliberately by the translators but crept in by negligence, the Greeks writing numbers in letters; weigh the reports about the graves and decline to affirm anything for certain, allowing that empty tombs may have stood for some; and object that the sentence does not concern Jacob at all.

debates: How the seventy-five souls stand to the seventy of the Hebrew: a straightforward following of the Greek version (Barnes, Clarke, Robertson, Wesley), an uncritical acceptance of it by a Hellenistic speaker (Ellicott), a possible corruption within the Greek version itself (Calvin), or evidence that its books had different translators (Lightfoot).

How the burial at Sychem is to be reconciled with the burial at Machpelah: a rhetorical compression of two events (Wesley), a Samaritan tradition the speaker followed (Ellicott), a standoff between equally weighted authorities (Clarke), an open question (Calvin), or an error in the text to be mended by conjecture (Robertson).
Whether the sentence includes Jacob at all — Gill denies it, Ellicott says the words appear to include him, Robertson allows that the subject may be the fathers only.
outliers: Ellicott alone attributes the numerical difference to the speaker’s own want of investigation rather than to a textual question.
Calvin alone suspects the Greek translators’ number of being a copying accident, and gives the palaeographical reason.
Lightfoot alone infers from the discrepancy that the books of the Greek version had more than one translator.
Robertson alone contemplates emending the New Testament text by conjecture, citing the count of primitive errors in it.

17.pericope_label: The people multiply; Moses is born, exposed, taken up by Pharaoh’s daughter and taught all the wisdom of the Egyptians

schools.summary: Make the unequal rate of the people’s increase the lesson, providence moving fastest as it nears its end, so that slowness earlier is no ground of discouragement.

Set the birth against the decree that should have prevented it, and take the moment when nothing can be hoped from men as the fittest for God to work; deny that Moses was a magician; and press the danger of the Egyptian training along with the questions unbelief raises about the delay of the deliverance.

Explain the description of the child as a Hebrew superlative, or reject that and construe it of urbanity as God regarded him; identify the verb of taking up as the term for adopting a foundling; describe the content of Egyptian learning and its transmission westward; and observe that Scripture nowhere states the education, which rests on later tradition and serves as a plea for secular learning.

Give the list of Egyptian sciences and report the rabbinic identification of that wisdom with magic; read the exposure as the means by which the deliverer was bred for a kingdom; and distinguish weight of speech from readiness of utterance.

debates: What the description of the infant means: a Hebrew superlative for very handsome (Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott) or, on the etymology and the force of the dative, fair as God regarded him and marked by city polish rather than beauty (Robertson).
Whether the wisdom Moses learned included magic — reported from the rabbis by Clarke, expressly denied by Gill.
Whether the education is a fact of the sacred history at all: Ellicott alone notes that the Pentateuch does not state it and traces it to a half-legendary tradition.
How “mighty in words” stands with Moses’ own confession of slow speech — Wesley alone distinguishes weight from readiness.
outliers: Robertson alone abandons the received sense of the adjective and derives it from the word for a city.
Ellicott alone reads the passage as an argument for the value of secular learning, comparing later Christian apologists.
Calvin alone treats the Egyptian education as a hazard needing to be overruled, and alone states the objections unbelief raises against the delay.
Henry alone reasons from the two unequal halves of the interval to a rule about the pace of providence.

23.pericope_label: Moses at forty visits his brethren, avenges the oppressed, is refused, and flees into Midian

schools.summary: Mark the age as coming from tradition and not from Scripture; read the visit as a late awakening rather than a lifelong attachment, the deliverer having long neglected his brethren; ground the expectation of recognition on the public facts of his birth and rank; and lay the guilt of the refusal on the whole people, whose silence made one man’s insolence their own.

Report the tradition of the three forty-year periods and show it to be a received schema told of others besides Moses; deny that the conjunction means “for”, which would make the killing deliberate; correct the tense of the attempted reconciliation and the form of the address; and credit the speaker’s account of Moses’ prophetic consciousness to good authority outside Scripture.

Hold that the desire to deliver was infused early by the Spirit and issued in the renunciation of the Egyptian crown; explain the expectation of recognition by a commission the people should have received as Moses had; and attribute the failure to their stupidity and sloth.

debates: Whether Moses was long attached to his nation or long estranged from it: Clarke has the desire infused early and shown in his refusal of the crown, Calvin reads the visit as the awaking of a mind that had neglected them.

How the conjunction at the twenty-fifth verse is to be rendered, and so whether the killing of the Egyptian was deliberate — Ellicott denies the received “for” on the ground that it imports a deliberateness the Exodus narrative does not have.

On what authority the age of forty and the prophetic consciousness of Moses rest, both being absent from Scripture: tradition (Gill, Barnes, Clarke), a schema applied to several sages (Lightfoot on the first), good authority and national consent (Lightfoot on the second).
Whether the guilt of the refusal is one man’s or the whole people’s — Calvin argues the second from their silence.
outliers: Lightfoot alone shows the threefold forty to be a stock pattern told of later rabbis, and so a schema rather than a chronology.
Ellicott alone lets a single conjunction decide the moral character of the killing.
Calvin alone denies that Moses had always owned his people, against the sense he says many take.
Lightfoot alone attributes a prophetic consciousness to Moses while still in the Egyptian court.

30.pericope_label: The bush that burned and was not consumed; I am the God of thy fathers; I have seen the affliction of my people

schools.summary: Take the honour paid to Moses here as itself the answer to the charge of blaspheming him, and read the forty years’ delay as designed, so that the deliverance should plainly be God’s work and not the deliverer’s.

Reckon the eighty years from tradition; weigh what the exchange of a court for a shepherd’s office would have cost, and the doubts it must have raised; explain that God authenticates his visions so that they may be told from Satan’s counterfeits; and account for the divine titles as condescensions to senses that cannot bear the bare majesty.

Reconcile the two names of the mountain as peaks of one range and identify the shrub; take the angel of the bush for Jehovah and the eternal Word, or else lay down the contrary rule that visible manifestations are angelic and audible ones are of the Word; and read the quotation as a thrust at the Sadducees on the bench, whom Christ had already met with it.
Identify the angel with the Son of God on the ground that he calls himself Jehovah; and pass the passage over to the exposition of the parallel narrative.
Use the same words to prove a life to come against opponents who receive the Law only, the title implying that those named have being and subsistence.

debates: Who appeared in the bush: the angel is Jehovah himself and the eternal Word (Robertson, Wesley), or the visible manifestation is angelic while the voice alone is of the Word (Ellicott’s rule, which reverses the arrangement).
Whether Sinai and Horeb are the same mountain — Barnes and Robertson answer that they are peaks of one range, Ellicott treats it as a simple substitution of the familiar name.

What the quotation is doing in this speech: recalling the covenant with the fathers (Gill, Barnes), proving the resurrection against Sadducees (Robertson, Ellicott), or proving a life to come from the Law alone against those who reject the prophets (Cyril).
Why God takes a title from the fathers at all — Calvin alone answers from the incapacity of human sense for unclothed majesty.
outliers: Ellicott alone lays down a general rule distinguishing what is seen in a theophany from what is heard, and alone places the speaker’s quotation inside the party divisions of the court trying him.
Henry alone argues from the honour paid to Moses in the speech that the charge of blaspheming him is refuted by the speech itself.
Calvin alone asks how a genuine vision is to be told from a counterfeit, and makes the answer a condition of faith in any oracle.
Cyril alone applies the verse against opponents who accept only the Pentateuch.

35.pericope_label: This Moses whom they refused, God sent to be ruler and deliverer; a prophet like unto me; the church in the wilderness

schools.summary: Count the rhetorical repetition and read the whole passage as a parallel between Moses and Jesus, pressed in the rare noun for deliverer; mark the point at which the court would have caught the drift and infer the effect on the style of what follows; defend or reject “church” as the rendering of the assembly; and note that the Exodus narrative mentions no angel at the giving of the law.
Set the refusal of Moses beside the hearers’ own generation disowning their king, and press the identity of the one rejected and afterwards sent.

Answer the objection that these men did not refuse Moses by the imputation of the fathers’ sin to children of the same spirit; identify the angel as no created angel, since he took the divine name; declare that Moses announced the very prophet they had killed; and explain why the oracles are called living.

Take the refusal as proof that the deliverance was undeserved, God delivering them as it were against their will; hold that the passage proves Christ to be the end of the law though it does not say so in terms, while allowing that the prophecy also fits the other prophets; and find in the wilderness assembly a pledge that God always has a church.

debates: Whether the assembly in the wilderness should be called a church or a congregation: Ellicott defends the received word and gives the history of the earlier versions, Robertson prefers congregation.

How the law can be said to have been given by an angel when the narrative ascribes it to God: the angel designates him who was God (Barnes), Moses mediated between the angel and the people (Clarke, Robertson), and Robertson adds that Exodus mentions no angel.
Whether the hearers can be charged with a refusal made by their fathers — Wesley alone raises and answers it.
How far the prophecy of a prophet like Moses is exclusively of Christ — Calvin holds it proves Christ the end of the law while agreeing also to the other prophets.
outliers: Chrysostom alone pairs the taunt against Moses with the hearers’ own disowning of their king.
Ellicott alone reads a change in the style of the later verses as evidence that the court had begun to interrupt.
Calvin alone says the people were delivered against their will.
Robertson alone observes that the source narrative supplies no angel for the giving of the law.

39.pericope_label: The fathers turn back to Egypt and make a calf; God gives them up to the host of heaven; Moloch and Remphan

schools.summary: Mark the repetition of the word for thrusting away; argue from the Hebrew that the calf broke the second commandment and not the first; state the inconsistency between the prophet’s question and the Pentateuch; supply the Pauline parallel for the giving-up; canvass the identifications of the two idols and report that some take one word for statues rather than a name; and cite a rabbinic dispute in which this verse was already a proof-text.
Read the abandonment as the punishment of the earlier sin and the pattern of the later giving-up of the heathen world to a reprobate mind.

Find the aggravation in the direction of the longing, back toward a bondage lately escaped, and in a return made in mind rather than in body; and describe the first fall as the entrance to a labyrinth, one idol multiplying into many by just vengeance.

Grant that sacrifices were offered in the wilderness and deny that they were offered uprightly; set the Greek and Hebrew of the idol names side by side and pronounce the place obscure; identify the two gods with planets; and notice that the threatened exile has been carried from Damascus to Babylon.

debates: How the prophet’s question can stand when the Pentateuch records sacrifices in the wilderness: an inconsistency to be acknowledged (Ellicott), sacrifices offered but not uprightly and so not accepted (Clarke, Wesley), or a question already disputed in the schools (Lightfoot).

What the two idol names are: a tabernacle of Moloch and a star of Remphan, or Siccuth your king with Chiun — Clarke reports both texts and calls the place obscure, Ellicott inclines to the proper name, Robertson reports that some read statues rather than any name.
Whether the golden calf broke the first or the second commandment — Ellicott alone raises the question and answers the second.
Why the exile is said to be beyond Babylon when the prophet wrote beyond Damascus — noticed by Wesley alone.
outliers: Ellicott alone determines which commandment the calf transgressed, on the number of the Hebrew noun.
Lightfoot alone shows the verse to have been a standing proof-text in a rabbinic dispute about sacrifice in the wilderness.
Wesley alone notices the alteration of the place of exile and assigns the fulfilment.
Robertson alone reads the whole preceding narrative as preparation for a blow still to come.

44.pericope_label: The tabernacle of witness made after the pattern, brought in with Joshua; David asks, Solomon builds

schools.summary: Explain the title of the tabernacle and the Greek version’s use of it; note that the phrase was suggested by the idol’s tabernacle just before, and that the argument now turns to the freedom of God from any one place; state the concession and its limit, that the sanction of tabernacle and temple is admitted but denied to be final; and prefer the Hebrew form of the captain’s name while finding a gain in the ambiguity here.

Confine the testimony to the two tables; insist that the name should always be rendered Joshua in such places; explain the refusal to David by the wars and the blood; and observe that the petition was not granted, God remaining without a temple till the son built one.

Give both names of the tabernacle and both reasons; clear God of blame for the people’s errors, since he had prescribed the manner of his worship, and charge them with adding to the rule and with losing sight of the end of the temple; and defend Solomon from the suspicion of having misconceived the nature of God.

debates: Whether the Greek name in the forty-fifth verse should be turned into Joshua: Barnes and Clarke say it should, Ellicott concedes the general rule but finds a gain in leaving the identity of the two names visible.

What the speech concedes about the temple and what it withholds — Ellicott states the concession and the limit twice, Clarke reads the whole as a rebuke of reliance on outward privilege, Calvin as an acquittal of God rather than an attack on the building.
Whether the speech reflects on Solomon — Calvin raises the suspicion and answers that Solomon knew God was to be sought in heaven, and that the work was commanded and promised.
What David asked for: a tent or a house — Robertson distinguishes the words, Wesley notes the petition was refused.
outliers: Ellicott alone observes that the name of Jesus occurs in the whole defence only in the Greek form of Joshua’s name.
Robertson alone traces the phrase to the idol’s tabernacle named a few lines earlier, and alone reports the papyrus evidence about the word for a successor.
Calvin alone defends Solomon by name against an inference the speech might seem to invite.

48.pericope_label: The Most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands: heaven is my throne and earth my footstool

schools.summary: Refer the doctrine to Solomon’s own words at the dedication, the divine majesty being uncontainable by the whole compass of nature; and reconstruct the interruption, the hearers raising a clamour once they saw what conclusions were coming.

Deny that the language about sitting implies body or parts, the point being incomprehensibility by place; warn against measuring God or his worship by human nature; conclude that God needs nothing we offer and that true worship is therefore not contained in ceremonies; and note that the prophet’s words are an assertion where the speech makes them a question.

Admit that the reason for the remark is not clear and then state what it achieves, that a house God does not need may be destroyed; observe that the true text speaks of things made with hands and not of temples; trace the doctrine to a possible Samaritan connection; and draw out the universality it establishes, together with the effect it had on the court.

debates: Why the denial is introduced at this point, having just conceded the divine sanction of the temple — Barnes says the reason is not very clear and argues only from the consequence.
Where the speaker’s doctrine of the temple comes from: Solomon’s own prayer (Clarke, Wesley, Gill, Robertson), or an echo of Samaritan opinion reaching him by some connection (Ellicott).
Whether the closing words are a question or an assertion — Gill notes that the prophet states them without the interrogation.

What the passage establishes: that this temple might be destroyed (Barnes), that its holiness was never exclusive (Ellicott), that worship is spiritual and universal (Robertson), or that ceremonies are no part of true worship at all (Calvin).
outliers: Barnes alone confesses that he cannot see why the remark is introduced where it is.
Ellicott alone accounts for the doctrine by the speaker’s supposed connection with the Samaritans.
Robertson alone treats the strength of the argument as the cause of the violence that answered it.
Clarke alone reconstructs the interruption and makes it the reason the tone of the speech changes.

51.pericope_label: Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost; which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?

schools.summary: Read the change of tone as the mark of an interruption, or refuse that inference and account for it by the natural climax of the argument; trace both epithets to the older Scriptures and turn the second against men who boasted of exclusive privilege; and weigh the title of the Just One, which was not among the received names of the Messiah.

Reconstruct the unspoken conclusion, that the temple service must give way to worship in spirit and truth, and explain the outbreak by the hearers’ willingness to hear their history and unwillingness to hear its application.

Hold that more was to have been said, the long approach having been designed to tame the hearers, and place the outbreak at the proof that law and temple alike had been corrupted; and take the stiff neck for a refusal of the yoke of God’s law.

Derive the first epithet from oxen that will not bend to the yoke and the second from the meaning of circumcision; read both as predictions fulfilled in the verses immediately following; and give two grounds for the title of the Just One, the integrity of the life and the acquittal before Pilate.
Set against the charge of resisting the Spirit the fact that those who disputed with this speaker could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke.

debates: Whether the speech was interrupted here: Barnes, Ellicott, Henry and Calvin all infer an interruption from the change of tone, while Robertson answers that the natural climax explains it without one.
Whether the charge that they persecuted every prophet is literally true — Barnes says it is a national characteristic and not a universal fact.
Whether “the Just One” was a current title of the Messiah — Ellicott doubts it and traces its adoption to the church at Jerusalem, while Clarke grounds it in the life and in the judicial acquittal.
Whether the two epithets describe the hearers or predict what they are about to do — Wesley alone takes them as predictions.
outliers: Robertson alone denies that an interruption need be assumed to explain the change of tone.
Lightfoot alone supplies a rabbinic story in which the same rebuke, in the same words, was answered by killing the man who gave it.
Ellicott alone notes that the reproach of an uncircumcised heart had been aimed at strangers and is here turned on those who claimed exclusive privilege.
Clarke alone grounds the title of the Just One in a Roman magistrate’s verdict.

54.pericope_label: They gnash on him with their teeth; he sees the glory of God and the Son of man standing at the right hand

schools.summary: Render the verb of the fifty-fourth verse as a sawing through and mark the gnashing as the single literal use of a familiar figure, expressing brute passion; hold the vision to have been inward and explain how the report of it reached the writer; note that the posture is standing where elsewhere it is sitting; observe that the title of the Son of man occurs certainly nowhere else outside the Gospels; and trace the words to the vision of Daniel, where a rabbinic commentator reads them of the Messiah.

Trace the proceeding from a colour of judgment through interruption to cries meant to drown every further word, and call the result madness rather than anger; deny that the heavens were changed at all, a new quickness of sight having been granted to one man only; and read the upward look as the recourse of a man destitute of every human help.
Set the scene as hell and heaven serving as foils to each other, and note that no vote, verdict or sentence of the court is recorded.
Give the same violent sense to the verb; explain the standing as a readiness to receive the martyr, or as the Mediator’s official posture, while allowing that elsewhere he is said to sit.
Turn the fury back on the accusers, since the man wronged had the better right to be angry and used no calumny; and, on the clause itself, amass the testimonies that the Son sits at the right hand.

debates: Whether anything happened outwardly: Calvin denies any change in the heavens and grants only a new power of sight to one man, and Ellicott likewise makes the vision inward, drawing from it that the council saw nothing and took the claim for further blasphemy.

Why the Son is standing where he is elsewhere seated: a rising to cheer the dying man (Robertson), a readiness to receive him (Wesley), or the posture of his mediatorial office (Clarke) — while Cyril collects the witnesses for the sitting.
Whether the proceeding was ever a trial at all — Henry notes that no vote, verdict or sentence is recorded.
How the vision could be reported when only one man saw it — Ellicott alone answers, from the martyr’s face and from his words.
outliers: Ellicott alone notices that the gnashing of teeth is used literally here and figuratively everywhere else, and alone accounts for the transmission of a vision nobody else witnessed.
Chrysostom alone argues that the accused had the better title to indignation than his judges.
Cyril alone gathers the evidence against the posture the verse describes.
Lightfoot alone produces a Jewish commentator who reads the Daniel vision of the Messiah.

57.pericope_label: They stop their ears, cast him out of the city and stone him; the witnesses lay their clothes at Saul’s feet

schools.summary: Distinguish the crowd from the court; choose between a feigned zeal and a real torment at hearing Christ glorified, and prefer the second; and measure the sentence against the law it claimed, which defines a false prophet as one who draws the people to strange gods, so that the death was unjust and the martyr suffers the punishment of the wicked, the cause alone making the difference.

Hold that it was a popular tumult in which no vote was taken, and account for the absence of Roman restraint; note nevertheless that the legal forms of place and of the witnesses’ part were observed; and supply the rabbinic rule that fixed the place of stoning outside three camps.

Deny that any sentence was passed, the stoning coming first and the justification after; read the stopped ears as an admission that the words, if true, convicted the hearers of murder; and turn to the young man who kept the clothes and the cause he would afterwards die in.

debates: How far the death was a judicial act: no sentence at all (Wesley, Clarke), a tumult in which no vote was taken and Roman restraint happened to be absent (Robertson, Ellicott), or an irregular condemnation in which the forms of place and manner were still kept (Barnes, supported by the rule Lightfoot supplies).

Why the ears were stopped: a pretence of hearing blasphemy (Robertson), an unwillingness to hear what would convict them of murder (Clarke), or a rage that could not bear to hear Christ glorified (Calvin, choosing against a feigned zeal).
Whether the stoning answered to the law it invoked — Calvin alone tests it against the statutory definition of a false prophet and finds it does not.
outliers: Lightfoot alone gives the rabbinic reckoning of the three camps that fixed where a stoning might take place.
Ellicott alone compares the scene with a later church council and with the apostolic rule that a bishop must not be a striker.
Robertson alone proposes a gap between Roman governors as the occasion.
Wesley alone addresses the bystander who held the clothes and sets his later death beside this one.

59.pericope_label: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit; Lord, lay not this sin to their charge; and he fell asleep

schools.summary: Show that the word “God” is an insertion absent from every ancient copy, so that the prayer is addressed to Christ, and support the point from a Roman governor’s report of Christian worship; note that the stoning continued through the prayer and that the kneeling was worship; argue from the resemblance to the dying prayer of Christ that the crucifixion narrative was already known to the speaker; and set the expression for death against its rabbinic parallels.

Deny the genuineness of the same word on manuscript and patristic evidence, and infer that prayer is here offered to Christ in the most solemn circumstance possible; argue that such an act of worship could not be paid to a creature; and read the second prayer as the disciple closely copying his Master.

Find in the law that made the witnesses cast the first stone a check that these men overrode, having already killed with their tongues; note that some show of judgment survived even in the tumult; and observe that the prayer for enemies was made at the moment when revenge would most naturally have been desired.

debates: What follows from the absence of the word “God” from the text: that the prayer was addressed to Christ and is therefore an act of divine worship — argued independently by Barnes, Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott.

Whether the resemblance between this prayer and the dying prayer of Christ is imitation or evidence: Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Calvin treat it as the mind of Christ reproduced, while Ellicott makes it proof that the crucifixion narrative was already known to the speaker.
Whether “fell asleep” is a distinctively scriptural way of describing a saint’s death (Barnes) or a common rabbinic idiom (Lightfoot).
Whether the proceeding retained any judicial character — Calvin allows a show of judgment in the witnesses casting the first stones.
outliers: Ellicott alone treats the likeness of the two prayers as a question of literary dependence, and alone names the accuser he thinks the prayer was chiefly for.
Calvin alone explains why the law required the witnesses to throw first, and turns their willingness into the measure of their guilt.
Lightfoot alone shows the language of falling asleep to be common in the rabbinic writers.
